questions.question: How do you handle exceptions with begin/rescue/ensure in Ruby?
questions.title: begin, rescue, and ensure
questions.direct_answer: begin/rescue/ensure is Ruby's exception handling: begin wraps code that may raise; rescue catches a class of exception (StandardError by default); ensure runs cleanup whether or not an exception occurred (like finally). You rescue specific classes (rescue ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound) not bare rescue (which catches StandardError and hides bugs). The pattern: begin; do work; rescue SpecificError => e; handle; ensure; close the file/connection; end. rescue without a class catches StandardError (not Exception), which is usually what you want but should still be specific where possible.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know begin wraps, rescue catches (StandardError by default), ensure always runs (cleanup), and to rescue specific classes.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Bare rescue (catches everything, hides bugs) or rescuing Exception (catches SystemExit, breaks signal handling).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: begin wraps; rescue catches a class (StandardError default); ensure always runs (cleanup). Rescue specific classes, not bare rescue or Exception.

sections.title: Wrap, Catch, Always Clean Up
sections.content: begin, rescue, and ensure is Ruby's exception handling. begin wraps code that may raise; rescue catches a class of exception (StandardError by default); ensure runs cleanup whether or not an exception occurred, like finally in other languages. You rescue specific classes — rescue ActiveRecord colon colon RecordNotFound — not a bare rescue, which catches StandardError and hides bugs. The pattern: begin; do the work; rescue SpecificError arrow e; handle it; ensure; close the file or connection; end. rescue without a class catches StandardError, not Exception, which is usually what you want but should still be specific where possible so you don't swallow unexpected errors.

sections.title: begin -> rescue -> ensure
sections.content:
Work runs; on raise, rescue catches; ensure always runs.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  B[begin: work] -->|ok| A[after]
  B -->|raise| R[rescue: catches]
  R --> A
  B --> E[ensure: cleanup]
  R --> E
  E --> A
```

sections.title: begin/rescue/ensure
sections.content:
```ruby
def read_config(path)
  file = nil
  begin
    file = File.open(path)            # may raise
    config = file.read
    parse(config)                     # may raise
  rescue Errno::ENOENT => e           # specific: file not found
    puts "config missing: #{e.message}"
    {}
  rescue JSON::ParserError => e       # specific: bad JSON
    puts "bad config: #{e.message}"
    {}
  ensure
    file&.close                        # ALWAYS runs, raise or not
  end
end

# AVOID bare rescue (hides bugs) and rescuing Exception:
#   rescue => e            # catches StandardError; too broad often
#   rescue Exception       # catches SystemExit too — DON'T
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Bare rescue (catches StandardError) — too broad; hides unexpected bugs.
Rescuing Exception (catches SystemExit, Interrupt) — breaks signal handling.
Forgetting ensure for cleanup (file/connection left open on an exception).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: begin wraps code that may raise; rescue catches a class (StandardError by default).
ensure ALWAYS runs, raise or not — use it for cleanup (close file/connection).
Rescue specific classes (RecordNotFound), not bare rescue or Exception.
rescue without a class catches StandardError (not Exception) — still prefer specific.
Don't rescue Exception — it catches SystemExit and breaks signal handling.
